In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Fatihah

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

He did not mention here any place or time for His praise. In Surat al-Rum He mentioned that among its places is the heavens and the earth, in His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth﴾. And in Surat al-Qasas He mentioned that among its times are this world and the Hereafter, in His saying: ﴿He is Allah; there is no deity except Him. To Him belongs praise in the first and the last [i.e., in this world and the Hereafter]﴾. And at the beginning of Surat Saba' He said: ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾. The definite article in (al-hamdu, "the praise") is for comprehensiveness, encompassing all praiseworthy qualities. It is a praise with which Allah, exalted is He, praised Himself, and within it He commanded His servants to praise Him with it.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. He did not specify here what the "worlds" (al-'alamin) are, but He clarified that in another place by His saying: ﴿Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" ﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 23, 24].

Some scholars said: the word 'alam (world) is derived from 'alamah (sign), because the existence of the world is an undoubted sign of the existence of its Creator, characterized by the attributes of perfection and majesty. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190]. And "ayah" (sign) in the language means "'alamah" (sign).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

These are two attributes of Allah, exalted is He, and two of His Most Beautiful Names (al-asma' al-husna), derived from mercy (al-rahmah) in the form of intensive emphasis (al-mubalaghah). Al-Rahman is more intensive in emphasis than al-Rahim, because al-Rahman is the One possessing all-encompassing mercy for all creatures in this world, and for the believers in the Hereafter, while al-Rahim is the One possessing mercy for the believers on the Day of Resurrection. This is the view of most scholars. In the speech of Ibn Jarir there is what implies the transmission of consensus upon this. In the tafsir of some of the early scholars (al-salaf) there is what indicates it, as Ibn Kathir said, and the narration transmitted from Jesus supports it, as Ibn Kathir and others mentioned, that he said, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace: "Al-Rahman is the Rahman of this world and the Hereafter, and al-Rahim is the Rahim of the Hereafter." (p-6) Allah, exalted is He, has pointed to what we have mentioned when He said: ﴿Then He istawa (established Himself) over the Throne, the Most Gracious﴾, and said: ﴿The Most Gracious, over the Throne He established Himself﴾. So He mentioned the istiwa' with His name al-Rahman so that His mercy would encompass all of His creation, as Ibn Kathir said. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them in? None holds them up except the Most Gracious﴾, meaning: and from His being Rahman is His gentleness toward the birds, and His holding them aloft, spreading and folding their wings in the air of the sky. Among the clearest evidences for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Gracious, taught the Qur'an﴾ up to His saying: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾, and He said: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾, so He specified them with His name al-Rahim.

If it is said: how can what we have established be reconciled with what came in the transmitted supplication, from His saying (ﷺ): "Rahman of this world and the Hereafter and Rahim of both"? The apparent answer, and Allah knows best, is that al-Rahim is specific to the believers as we have mentioned, but it is not restricted to them in the Hereafter alone; rather it also includes their mercy in this world. So the meaning of "Rahimuhuma" ("Rahim of both") is His mercy toward the believers in both.

The proof that He is Merciful to the believers in this world as well is that this is the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He it is who showers blessings upon you, and His angels, that He may bring you out of darkness into light. And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾, because His blessing upon them, the blessing of His angels, and His bringing them out of darkness into light is mercy to them in this world, even if it is also the cause of mercy in the Hereafter. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly Allah turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a party of them had nearly inclined to deviate. Then He turned to them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is to them Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117]. In it came the preposition "bi" attached to "al-rahm" governing the pronoun referring to the Prophet (ﷺ), the Emigrants and the Helpers, and His turning to them in forgiveness is mercy in this world, even if it is also the cause of the mercy of the Hereafter. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Al-Shinqiti's commentary on the verse ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾:

And His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾.

He did not explain it here, but He explained it in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what is the Day of Judgment? Then, what will make you know what is the Day of Judgment? It is the Day when no soul will possess anything for [another] soul at all﴾ [al-Infitar: 17, 18, 19], and the verse continues.

The intended meaning of "ad-din" (recompense, judgment) in the verse is the recompense. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them their full recompense (dinahum al-haqq)﴾, meaning: the recompense of their deeds with justice.

(p-٧)His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You alone do we worship﴾

In this noble verse, He points to the realisation of the meaning of *Lā ilāha illā Allāh* (there is no deity except God), because its meaning is composed of two elements: negation and affirmation. The negation is the rejection of all objects of worship other than God, the Exalted, in all kinds of worship. The affirmation is the singling out of the Lord of the heavens and the earth alone for all kinds of worship in the manner prescribed. He pointed to the negation in *Lā ilāha illā Allāh* by placing forward the object, which is (إيّاكَ) (*iyyāka*, "You"), and this has been established in the *uṣūl* (principles of jurisprudence) in the discussion of *dalīl al-khiṭāb* (the argument from discourse), which is *mafhūm al-mukhālafa* (the implied meaning by contrast). And in the *ma'ānī* (the science of rhetoric), in the discussion of *qaṣr* (restriction), that the fronting of the object is one of the forms of restriction. He pointed to the affirmation from it by His saying: (نَعْبُدُ) (*na'budu*, "we worship").

The meaning indicated here has been explained in detail in other verses, such as His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you﴾ up to the end of the verse [Al-Baqarah: 21], where He stated the affirmation by His saying: ﴿worship your Lord﴾, and stated the negation at the end of the noble verse by His saying: ﴿So do not set up rivals to God while you know﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 22]. And as in His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship God and avoid ṭāghūt (false objects of worship)"﴾, where He stated the affirmation by His saying: ﴿Worship God﴾ and the negation by His saying: ﴿and avoid ṭāghūt﴾. And as in His saying: ﴿So whoever disbelieves in ṭāghūt and believes in God has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 256], where He stated the negation by His saying: ﴿whoever disbelieves in ṭāghūt﴾ and the affirmation by His saying: ﴿and believes in God﴾. And as in His saying: ﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except for He who created me"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 26–27]. And as in His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Al-Anbiyā': 25], and His saying: ﴿And ask those We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint deities other than the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 45], and other verses besides these.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And You alone do we ask for help﴾. That is: we seek help from You alone, because the whole matter is in Your hand alone, and none possesses with You any part of it, not even the weight of an atom. And His bringing, ﴿And You alone do we ask for help﴾, after His saying ﴿You alone do we worship﴾, contains an indication that one should not rely upon anyone except the one who deserves worship, because other than Him does not hold the matter in his hand. This meaning indicated here has come clearly explained in other verses:

• as in His saying: ﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him﴾ up to the end of the verse [Hūd: 123],

• and His saying: ﴿But if they turn away, say, "God is sufficient for me; there is no deity except Him. Upon Him I have relied"﴾ up to the end of the verse [At-Tawbah: 129],

• and His saying: ﴿Lord of the east and the west; there is no deity except Him, so take Him as a trustee﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 9],

and His saying:

(p-٨)﴿Say, "He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him, and upon Him we have relied"﴾ [Al-Mulk: 29], and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 7:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾

He did not specify here who those upon whom Allah bestowed favour are. He specified that in another place with His saying: ﴿Then those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour of the prophets, the truthful (al-siddiqin), the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾

Two admonitions (tanbihan)

The first: From this noble verse is derived the validity of the imamate (leadership) of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, because he is included among those whom Allah commanded us, in the seven oft-repeated (al-sab' al-mathani) and the Great Qur'an, meaning al-Fatihah, to ask Him to guide us to their path. This indicates that their path is the Straight Path.

This is in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray.﴾ He has specified those upon whom He bestowed favour, and among them He counted the siddiqin. The Prophet ﷺ has clarified that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, is among the siddiqin. It thus becomes clear that he is included among those upon whom Allah bestowed favour, whom Allah commanded us to ask for guidance to their path. There remains no ambiguity that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, is upon the Straight Path, and that his imamate is true.

The second: You have known that the siddiqin are among those upon whom Allah bestowed favour. Allah, Exalted, has explicitly stated that Maryam, daughter of 'Imran, is a siddiqah, in His saying: ﴿And her mother was a siddiqah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 75]. So, is Maryam included in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ or not?

The answer: Her inclusion among them is based on a well-known, disputed principle of usul al-fiqh, namely: do the sound masculine plural forms and similar forms found in the Great Qur'an and the Sunnah, which are specific to the group of males, include females, or do they not include them except by a separate indication? Some scholars held that they include females, and according to this, Maryam is included in the verse. The proponents of this view argued with two matters. The first: the consensus of the Arabic-speaking people on giving precedence to males over females in the plural.

The second: the occurrence of verses that indicate the inclusion of females in sound masculine plurals and the like, such as:

- His saying, Exalted is He, concerning Maryam herself: ﴿And she confirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devoutly obedient (al-qanitin)﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12];
- His saying concerning the wife of the minister: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this, and [you, woman], ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were among the wrongdoers (al-khati'in)﴾ [Yusuf: 29];
- His saying concerning Bilqis: ﴿And what she used to worship other than Allah had prevented her; indeed, she was of a disbelieving people﴾ [al-Naml: 43];
- and His saying, concerning what is like the sound masculine plural: ﴿We said, "Go down from it, all of you"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38], the verse, for Hawwa' is included in it by consensus.

Many scholars held that females are not included in this except by a separate indication. They cited verses such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women…﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]; and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts; that is purer for them﴾ [al-Nur: 31], then He said: ﴿And say to the believing women that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾, the verse [al-Nur: 31]. Their conjoining of the women to the men indicates that they are not included. They answered the argument of the first view by saying that giving precedence to males over females in the plural is not the point of dispute; rather the dispute concerns what is understood from the masculine plural and the like when used without qualification. As for the verses, they say that the inclusion of females in them is known only from the context and the indication of the wording; and their inclusion in cases accompanied by something that indicates this is not disputed.

According to this view, Maryam is not included in the verse. And to this disagreement the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud alluded in his saying:

[Rajaz meter]
"And is the inclusion of 'man' (man) of a female a deviation? And they differed regarding the like of 'the Muslims'."

* *

His saying: ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾. The majority of the scholars of tafsir said: ﴿those who have earned anger﴾ are the Jews, and ﴿those who are astray﴾ are the Christians. This has been reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ through the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim, may Allah be pleased with him. Although the Jews and the Christians are both astray and both have earned anger, anger has been specifically attributed to the Jews, even though the Christians share it with them, because they know the truth and deny it, and commit falsehood deliberately, so anger was their most distinctive attribute. The Christians are ignorant and do not know the truth, so going astray was their most distinctive attribute.

On this basis, that ﴿those who have earned anger﴾ are the Jews is clarified by His saying, Exalted is He, concerning them: ﴿So they returned bearing anger upon anger﴾, the verse [al-Baqarah: 90]; and His saying concerning them also: ﴿Shall I inform you of something worse than that as repayment from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has become angry﴾, the verse [al-Ma'idah: 60]; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by anger﴾, the verse [al-A'raf: 152]. And that ﴿those who are astray﴾ are the Christians is perhaps clarified by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the sound way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 77].
